findings.description: Vendored `wheel.cli.unpack` chmods a path built from the unsanitized archive member name (`zinfo.filename`) after `ZipFile.extract()`, allowing traversal outside the destination directory when unpacking a malicious wheel
findings.code_snippet:
with WheelFile(path) as wf:
        namever = wf.parsed_filename.group("namever")
        destination = Path(dest) / namever
        print(f"Unpacking to: {destination}...", end="", flush=True)
        for zinfo in wf.filelist:
            wf.extract(zinfo, destination)

            # Set permissions to the same values as they were set in the archive
            # We have to do this manually due to
            # https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/59999
            permissions = zinfo.external_attr >> 16 & 0o777
            destination.joinpath(zinfo.filename).chmod(permissions)
findings.reasoning: The `extract()` call at line 22 is a `zipfile.ZipFile.extract()` call, which internally sanitizes member names (strips leading `/`, drive letters, and `..` components), so the extraction itself is not traversal-prone. However, lines 29-30 then build a path from the RAW, unsanitized member name: `destination.joinpath(zinfo.filename).chmod(permissions)`. A wheel entry named `../../../../etc/shadow` (or any path outside `destination`) therefore results in `chmod()` being applied to an arbitrary attacker-chosen file on the host with attacker-controlled permission bits (e.g. 0o777). This is a genuine but strongly mitigated issue: (1) it is vendored third-party code (`setuptools/_vendor/wheel`), not part of setuptools' own runtime behavior; (2) it is only reachable via the `wheel unpack` CLI invoked by a user on a wheel they explicitly chose to unpack, i.e. an attacker must already convince the victim to unpack a malicious wheel — at which point arbitrary file content is already written. Impact is limited to permission changes (no arbitrary write/read). Classified as manual-review / low severity rather than a confirmed high-impact path traversal because it does not by itself write data outside the destination.

findings.reasoning: `setuptools/launch.py` is explicitly designed to run a Python script named on the command line: "Launch the Python script on the command line after setuptools is bootstrapped via import". The `compile()`/`exec()` pair executes the file identified by `sys.argv[1]`, which is exactly what `python <file>` does -- the invoking user already has full control over the Python process and, critically, the executed file. There is no privilege boundary crossed: the user who supplies argv[1] is the same principal running the interpreter, and executing a script they name grants no capability they did not already have. This is a documented, intentional feature (used for `python -m setuptools.launch <script>` bootstrapping of `setup.py`), not tainted deserialization or an injection sink reachable from a lower-privileged principal. The `__builtins__` reference on line 20 merely ensures the builtins module is loaded in the namespace so the exec'ed script inherits normal builtins.

findings.description: Unsafe `marshal.load()` of a `.pyc` file located via the module search path inside `get_module_constant` (CWE-502 deserialization of untrusted data); the surrounding recon query flags the whole marshal/compile/dis.Bytecode call chain in setuptools/depends.py
findings.code_snippet:
with maybe_close(f):
            if kind == PY_COMPILED:
                f.read(8)  # skip magic & date
                code = marshal.load(f)
findings.reasoning:
`get_module_constant()` calls `find_module(module, paths)` and, when the located file is a byte-compiled module (`kind == PY_COMPILED`), feeds it straight into `marshal.load(f)`. `marshal` is explicitly documented as not safe for untrusted data. The query group (py/dump-depends-calls) enumerated all sinks reachable on this path: Attribute() at 113/132/133/135/137/140, find_module() at 125, maybe_close() at 130, compile() at 137, and marshal.load() at 133.

Assessment: this is the *same trust boundary* as CPython's own import machinery (importlib/zipimport also marshal.load .pyc files), so an attacker who can plant a crafted .pyc on `paths`/sys.path can generally get code execution simply by having the module imported instead. There is therefore no clear privilege gain, which is why this is not a clean true positive. However, two facts keep it worth manual review:
  * `paths` is caller-supplied and `Require(...).get_version(paths)`/`is_present(paths)` accepts arbitrary directories; a third-party setup.py or tool that resolves dependency versions against an attacker-influenced directory would marshal.load an arbitrary blob before any import-time safeguards.
  * `marshal.load` on crafted bytes can also cause interpreter-level crashes/memory unsafety (not just logical deserialization), and malformed .pyc magic/date headers are not validated (only 8 bytes are skipped, no validation of `path`, size, or magic).
Recommendation: compare the read magic + flags against `importlib.util.MAGIC_NUMBER` before unmarshalling, use `marshal.loads` on a size-bounded buffer, and/or fall back to source parsing (`compile(f.read(), path, 'exec')`, which is already used for PY_SOURCE and is far safer).

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source: file handle returned by _imp.find_module(module, paths) where 'paths' is user/caller supplied (Require.get_version(paths) -> line 80). Sink: marshal.load(f) at line 133. No validation of pyc magic number, file size, or origin occurs between find_module and marshal.load; only 8 header bytes are skipped. Downstream, the resulting code object is walked with dis.Bytecode(code) in extract_constant (lines 145-185), which is not a sanitizer for the deserialization itself.
evidence.notes: Recon query py/dump-depends-calls reported the individual calls on this path (113 Attribute, 125 find_module, 130 maybe_close, 132/133/135/137/140 Attribute, 137 compile). Those individual call-site 'results' are observations, not vulnerabilities; the only genuine CWE-502 sink on the path is marshal.load at line 133 (compile() of PY_SOURCE at 137 is not equivalent to eval and is the safer branch).

findings.reasoning: In get_module_constant, when find_module locates a PY_SOURCE module on the caller-supplied `paths`, the source is read and passed to compile(..., 'exec').
